title: Courthouse Wedding Attire
metaTitle: Courthouse Wedding Attire for Guests: Court Rules, Day Dress
metaDescription: Courthouse wedding attire for guests: business casual to dressy casual, plus the court rules that apply. What women and men wear, and what security changes.
h1: Courthouse Wedding Attire: What Guests Wear to a City Hall or Civil Ceremony
answer: Dress for a smart daytime lunch: business casual to dressy casual. Women wear a knee-length or midi dress, a skirt with a blouse, or a tailored pantsuit. Men wear a sport coat or blazer with slacks, tie optional, or a dark suit if the couple is in one. The courtroom's own rules also apply: no hats, sunglasses, shorts, tank tops or flip-flops. And no white.
intro:
Courthouse wedding attire has one thing no other wedding dress code has: a second set of rules that nobody at the wedding wrote. The ceremony happens in a working government building, often in a courtroom, and the court's dress and conduct rules apply to everyone who walks in, guests included. Those rules are usually short and practical, and they ban things like hats, shorts and flip-flops. Above that floor, the couple's own clothes and the time of day decide how dressy you go.

This guide to courthouse wedding attire is for guests, women and men, at a courthouse, city hall or other civil ceremony. It takes three real sources and puts them together: the published courtroom attire rules of US courts, the Emily Post Institute's garment lists for business casual and dressy casual, and the wedding pages of two county courts that marry couples every weekday. The usual pattern is a short ceremony, a lunch and sometimes a party that night, so the guide also covers whether one outfit can do all three.

contentSections.heading: The courtroom sets a floor before the couple sets anything
contentSections.content:
A wedding at a hotel or a barn has one source of rules: the couple. A courthouse has two. Before anyone has said what to wear, the court has already said what not to wear, and its rules cover everyone in the room.

The wording varies but the intent is the same. The Justice of the Peace #3 court in Comal County, Texas, publishes this: "All persons present in the Courtroom shall be dressed in a manner that shows dignity and respect for the Court." Justices of the peace in Texas perform weddings, and that sentence covers a guest at one just as it covers anyone at a hearing. The federal court for the Southern District of Georgia applies its dress code to "individuals entering the United States Courthouses" in its district. The Eastern District of Texas has a separate paragraph headed "Spectators", which is what a wedding guest in a courtroom is.

Two things follow. First, the floor is about casual clothing, not formality: no court rule read for this page bans a suit, a dress or a gown. Second, the floor is enforced by a bailiff or security officer, not by a sulking relative. Comal County says the rules cover the courtroom, the reception or foyer area and the jury room, so a guest in a ball cap and shorts may be stopped before reaching the ceremony at all.

contentSections.heading: What the court lists actually ban
contentSections.content:
Put the three published lists side by side and the overlap is clear. These are the items that appear on at least one of them:

• Hats. Banned in the courtroom by Comal County and the Eastern District of Texas. If you wear a head covering for religious or medical reasons, ask the clerk's office before the day.
• Shorts and cut-offs. On all three lists.
• Tank tops, muscle shirts, T-shirts and sleeveless shirts. Each appears on at least one list; Georgia's federal courts include "sleeveless shirts".
• Flip-flops and bare feet. Comal County and the Eastern District of Texas ban flip-flops; Georgia bans bare feet.
• Anything revealing. "Mid-riff baring or other revealing or low cut clothing" and "extremely short skirts" (Eastern District of Texas); a "bare mid-section" (Southern District of Georgia).
• Sunglasses. Eastern District of Texas, for spectators.
• Slogans and pictures. Comal County bans clothing with "offensive, vulgar" words or images; Georgia requires offensive writing or tattoos to be covered.

Comal County adds one rule that catches men out: "All shirts must be tucked inside pants!" An untucked linen shirt that would be fine at the lunch afterwards is, in that courtroom, a breach.

Jeans need a closer read. The Eastern District of Texas bans "jeans or other denim pants" for jurors and witnesses, but its spectator list leaves them off. So denim is not banned for guests there, but the court plainly sees it as less than respectful. If the couple has not said casual, leave the jeans at home.

contentSections.heading: Above the floor: business casual to dressy casual
contentSections.content:
Once the court's floor is cleared, the question for courthouse wedding attire becomes how dressy to go. Courthouse weddings often come without a printed dress code, and the Emily Post Institute's advice for that situation is general: "The wedding invitation and the time of the wedding will be your best guide to its formality." Courthouse ceremonies are almost always in the daytime and usually small, which points to two neighbouring codes on Emily Post's attire guide.

Business casual, women: "Skirt, khakis, or pants"; "Open-collar shirt, knit shirt or sweater (no spaghetti straps or décolleté)"; "Dress".
Business casual, men: "Seasonal sport coat or blazer with slacks or khakis"; a dress shirt, button-down, open-collar or polo shirt; "Optional tie"; "Loafers or loafer-style shoes, and socks".

Dressy casual, women: "Dress"; "Skirt and dressy top"; "Dressy pants outfit"; "Nice jeans and dressy top".
Dressy casual, men: "Seasonal sport coat or blazer, and slacks"; a dress shirt, button-down, open-collar or polo shirt; "Optional tie".

For a courthouse wedding, aim at the overlap of the two lists and lean towards dressy casual, because it is still a wedding. In practice: a dress or polished separates for women, and a jacket with slacks for men. Emily Post's informal daytime wedding guidance says much the same: an "afternoon dress; dressy skirt or pants and blouse" for women, and a "sports jacket or blazer, slacks, tie optional" for men.

Business casual and dressy casual each have a full guide on this site if the invitation uses either term. For dresses, see business casual wedding guest dresses.

contentSections.heading: Ceremony, lunch, party: one outfit or three?
contentSections.content:
Many courthouse weddings run in three parts. A ceremony of a few minutes, a meal at a nearby restaurant, and sometimes a larger party later that day or on another date. The three settings have different rules, and the strictest one is the courthouse.

The practical answer is to dress for the courthouse and adjust from there. An outfit that passes the court lists and sits at dressy casual will also suit a midday restaurant. If the party starts after 6 p.m., Emily Post's advice is to "err on the side of formality", which for most guests means one change: men add a tie or switch to a dark suit, and women swap to a cocktail dress or dressier shoes and jewellery.

The table below shows what changes at each stop.

contentSections.heading: Weekday daytime is the default, so dress for daylight
contentSections.content:
Courts marry people in office hours. Justice of the Peace Court 1 in Tarrant County, Texas, holds ceremonies "during normal business hours only. Monday - Friday 8 a.m. - 4 p.m." and says the judge "does not conduct ceremonies after hours or on weekends." Clark County District Court in Washington holds them "every weekday at 4:30pm". Other offices may keep other hours, but at both of these courts you will almost always be dressing for a weekday ceremony in daylight.

That matters because time of day is the second half of Emily Post's rule, and daylight points down the formality scale. Daytime dress means lighter fabrics and colours in spring and summer, day shoes rather than evening sandals, and little shine: satin, sequins and heavy beading read as evening. For men, a blazer or a lighter suit fits better than a black one, though a dark suit is never wrong in a courtroom.

There is one exception. A late-afternoon ceremony that rolls straight into a dinner after 6 p.m. is effectively an evening event. Dress for the dinner, and make sure the outfit still clears the court's floor.

It also helps to remember that a weekday courthouse ceremony means many guests come from work or go back afterwards. Business casual from the office is acceptable at the ceremony; swapping one piece, a jacket or a pair of shoes, makes it look chosen for the day.

contentSections.heading: Getting through security in what you are wearing
contentSections.content:
Where a courthouse has a security station, every guest goes through the same screening as anyone with court business; a wedding party gets no separate entrance. The visitor policy of the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, which is typical of federal buildings, lists the steps:

• "Show a photo ID issued by a government agency."
• Put your "purse, briefcase, backpack, and other personal items" on the x-ray machine.
• Remove "keys, coins, wallets, and all other items in your pockets" before the magnetometer.
• "You may be asked to remove your belt, watch, jewelry, and shoes."

That last line is the one that affects your outfit. Shoes you can slip off and back on in a queue beat knee boots or lace-ups. Heavy metal hardware, chain belts and stacked bracelets slow you down. A small bag goes through faster than a large tote. Some courthouses also restrict what you can carry: the Southern District of Georgia does not allow bags or containers holding clothing unless you are there for court business, and restricts cameras and phones without approval. If you were planning to change between the ceremony and the party, check this first.

Allow extra time. Clark County asks everyone to arrive by 4:15 p.m. for a 4:30 ceremony, and the security line is part of the reason to be early. Bring a card rather than a boxed gift; it is easier to carry through the x-ray.

contentSections.heading: Small rooms and close photographs
contentSections.content:
A courthouse ceremony is small by rule, not just by choice. Tarrant County's courtroom holds "a maximum of 14 people, including children and photographers"; Clark County allows "no more than 10 guests" for occupancy reasons and says each ceremony "only takes a few minutes." Tarrant County also says the courtroom cannot be decorated, because it "remains an active workspace where official court business continues throughout the day."

Two things follow for guests. First, there are no flowers or decorations, just the courtroom itself, so the clothes carry the photographs. Most of those photos are close group shots of a handful of people. Solid colours and simple prints photograph better at that range than busy patterns, and a neat neckline matters more than a hemline nobody sees.

Second, you will be standing close to the couple in every picture. That is the practical reason to keep away from white and very pale neutrals: in a group of six, a cream dress next to the bride reads as a second bride.

Behaviour counts too. Tarrant County's wedding page lists quiet conversation while waiting, "No loud outbursts" and no "yelling, whistling, screaming or chanting," and reminds guests that "there are other Courts in Session." Save the cheering for the steps outside.

contentSections.heading: White, black, and the couple who ask for black tie
contentSections.content:
White. Emily Post's wedding guest page does not address it, so this site follows the etiquette expert Elaine Swann, who told TODAY: "Any shades of white, that color is still reserved for the bride. However, white is acceptable when the bride and groom ask you to wear it." A courthouse bride may be in a short white dress or a cream suit rather than a gown, which makes a white outfit on a guest more confusing, not less. Men are fine in a white dress shirt under a jacket.

Black. A "little black dress" is on Emily Post's semi-formal list for women, so black is acceptable at a wedding. In daylight, a black dress can look severe in close photos; colour in a jacket, shoe or bag lifts it. For men, a dark suit is the default at the formal end and is never wrong in a courtroom.

Black tie at a courthouse. It happens: some couples hold the legal ceremony at the courthouse and ask for black tie. When they do, the invitation wins, because Emily Post's rule is that the invitation is your best guide. No court list read for this page bans a tuxedo or a gown; they only ban the casual end. Expect stares in the security line and wear shoes you can walk in from the parking garage. The black tie guide on this site has the full lists.

contentSections.heading: For men: keep the jacket on
contentSections.content:
For male guests, the jacket matters more than anything else. The Eastern District of Texas says it directly in its spectator rules: "Men are required to wear coats." Not every court asks for one, but no court objects to one, and both Emily Post lists that fit a courthouse wedding, business casual and dressy casual, start with a sport coat or blazer.

A simple order of choices:

• If the couple is in a suit, or the evening plans are formal: a dark suit, dress shirt, tie, leather shoes.
• If the couple is dressed down or the invitation says casual: a navy blazer or seasonal sport coat with grey or tan trousers. Add a tie if you like; Emily Post lists it as optional.
• Shirt: a dress shirt or a button-down, tucked in. Comal County's "All shirts must be tucked inside pants!" applies to you.
• Shoes: loafers or leather lace-ups with socks. Loafers are easier at the x-ray.
• Leave in the car: a cap, sunglasses, shorts and flip-flops, each banned on at least one court list read for this page.

In summer, a linen or cotton blazer over an open collar keeps the jacket rule without the heat. In winter, take your overcoat off before the ceremony so the photographs show the jacket underneath. The wedding dress code for men page covers every other invitation wording.

contentSections.heading: A short note for the couple
contentSections.content:
This site writes for guests, but guests take their lead from the couple, so one paragraph is for you. Tell people what you are wearing. Many courthouse weddings have no printed invitation, so guests have nothing to work from on courthouse wedding attire except what they guess you will wear. One line in the group message sorts it out.

The court's rules apply to you too. A cap, sunglasses on the head or an untucked shirt can be stopped by a bailiff whether or not you are getting married. Check the guest limit (10 at Clark County, 14 including photographers at Tarrant County) before you invite anyone, and send guests the arrival time, not the ceremony time, so they clear security in time. If you are planning a party later, the full guide to what to wear to a wedding as a guest is a useful link to send.

faqs.question: Can you wear jeans to a courthouse wedding?
faqs.answer: Only if the couple says the dress code is casual. Emily Post lists "nice jeans and dressy top" under dressy casual for women and "good jeans" only under casual for men. One federal court, the Eastern District of Texas, bans "jeans or other denim pants" for jurors and witnesses, though not for spectators. Dark, clean jeans with a blazer or a dressy top are the most you should try, and only with the couple's go-ahead.

faqs.question: What should a guest wear to a city hall wedding with no dress code?
faqs.answer: Dress at dressy casual for the daytime: a knee-length or midi dress, a skirt and blouse, or a tailored pantsuit for women, and a sport coat or blazer with slacks, tie optional, for men. Emily Post's rule is that the invitation and the time of day are your best guide, and city hall ceremonies are almost always in office hours. Then check the court's own rules: no hats, shorts, tank tops or flip-flops.

faqs.question: Can I wear a hat to a courthouse wedding?
faqs.answer: Not inside the courtroom. Comal County's Justice of the Peace #3 and the Eastern District of Texas both list hats among the items not allowed. Take it off at the door and put it back on for photographs outside. If you wear a head covering for religious or medical reasons, ask the clerk's office before the day. Emily Post's guest guidance marks hats as optional "unless required", which a courtroom never does.
